description: Trepanation is the deliberate removal of a piece of the skull vault by scraping, grooving or drilling, first with stone tools. Healed bone edges show that many patients survived. description: Antiseptic surgery applied germ theory to wounds. uncertainty: Ignaz Semmelweis had cut childbed-fever deaths in Vienna by handwashing in 1847, before germ theory, but his explanation was not accepted. The shift from antiseptic to aseptic technique took place gradually in the 1880s-1890s.

description: Biomedical research is the continuing, organised effort to understand disease at the level of genes, cells and populations and to turn that understanding into treatment. Since the late twentieth century it has drawn on genome sequencing, large clinical trials and computing. Its results arrive unevenly: some conditions became treatable or preventable, while others, including many dementias, still resist.
uncertainty: As a repeatable node it stands for open-ended research rather than a dated discovery.

description: Endocrinology studies hormones, chemical messengers that glands release into the blood. In London in 1902, William Bayliss and Ernest Starling showed that secretin from the intestine triggers pancreatic secretion; Starling introduced the word hormone in 1905. In Toronto in 1922, a team of Frederick Banting, Charles Best, James Collip and John Macleod first treated a diabetic patient with purified insulin.
uncertainty: Gland extracts were used earlier (thyroid extract for myxoedema, 1891). Credit for insulin was disputed within the Toronto team.

description: Immunology studies the body's defences against infection and foreign material. In Berlin in 1890, Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō showed that serum from immunised animals neutralised diphtheria and tetanus toxins, founding serum therapy. In Vienna in 1901, Karl Landsteiner used the clumping of red cells by serum to identify blood groups, later central to transfusion and diagnosis.
uncertainty: Immunology has several roots (Metchnikoff's cellular theory, Ehrlich's antibody theory); the node dates it from serum therapy and serology.

description: Sulfonamides were the first synthetic drugs to cure common bacterial infections inside the body. At Bayer's laboratories in Elberfeld, Germany, Gerhard Domagk found in 1932 that the red dye Prontosil protected mice from streptococci; results appeared in 1935. Researchers in Paris then showed that the active part was sulfanilamide. Deaths from childbed fever fell from the mid-1930s.
uncertainty: Bayer was then part of IG Farben, and the chemists Klarer and Mietzsch synthesised the dye. Ehrlich's arsenical Salvarsan (1910) was an earlier synthetic antimicrobial, against syphilis.
